strengths: Addresses an important problem: imputing missing protected attributes can conceal bias in graph classifiers. The three-player adversarial formulation offers a plausible approach to generating more challenging imputations.
Reported results are encouraging, particularly on BAIL and GERMAN. On GERMAN, BFtS reduces the equality-of-opportunity gap from FairGNN’s 5.70% to 1.70% while maintaining F1 at 0.74.

Evaluation includes four real datasets, synthetic graphs, relevant FairGNN and RNF comparisons, GCN and GAT architectures, ten-run averages, fairness–accuracy trade-offs, and supplementary sensitivity studies. An anonymous code repository is linked.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees do not establish the behavior of the actual training objective. Proposition 1 and Theorem 1 analyze the adversarial objective after omitting the classification and imputation losses. An imputer minimizing L_I−βL_A need not maximize Jensen–Shannon divergence, and minimizing L_C+αL_A need not make that divergence zero. The admissible set underlying the supremum over imputations is also insufficiently specified.

The convergence argument contains mathematical errors. Appendix 5.3 states that distributions with disjoint supports have zero Jensen–Shannon divergence; their divergence is instead maximal. If all sensitive labels are identical, one conditional distribution is undefined. Furthermore, the divergence ordering in Corollary 1 does not establish improved gradients, stability, or convergence, and corresponding training diagnostics are absent.

Numerical inconsistencies undermine confidence in the evaluation. Figure 3(a) plots an RNF result near 1−ΔDP = −2, although Equation 9 requires this quantity to lie in [0,1]. Table 3 reports GERMAN F1 of 0.81 for the complete method, versus 0.74 in Table 1, without explaining the different setting. These discrepancies require reconciliation.

The experiments do not isolate the main methodological contribution. The LDAM ablations are useful, but there is no β=0 comparison disabling adversarial imputation under otherwise identical conditions, nor an LDAM-matched FairGNN baseline. Consequently, improvements cannot confidently be attributed to the additional adversarial interaction rather than the changed classification and imputation losses.

The missingness evaluation does not adequately test the motivating concern about biased data collection. Experiments vary the observed fraction from 20% to 50% of training nodes, but the selection mechanism is unclear and group-dependent or label-dependent missingness is not systematically evaluated. There is also no quantitative verification that the learned imputations approximate worst-case fairness or that conventional imputations systematically underestimate true bias.

Important implementation details are ambiguous or inconsistent. The manuscript does not explain differentiation through the binary imputed group assignments in Equation 3; Equation 2 uses classifier outputs in the imputation-loss denominator; and Figure 2’s caption reverses the classifier and adversary optimization directions relative to Equations 4–5. Validation/test partitions, optimizer settings, and training durations are insufficiently documented in the manuscript.
